first_check.explanation: The complaint is right that § 10-1-763(b) allows exemplary damages for willful and malicious misappropriation of up to 'twice' the compensatory award, so 'double' is accurate. There are two small defects. First, the complaint says the base is damages 'awarded under O.C.G.A. § 10-1-762', but § 10-1-762 governs injunctive relief; the base is the award under § 10-1-763(a). Second, that base covers actual loss, unjust enrichment, or a reasonable royalty, not only 'actual damages.' The rubric's claim that this is a misleading description, with a cap equal to actual damages, is itself wrong (see ref 20).

citations.authority: North Carolina Rule of Civil Procedure 4(j)(6)(a)
citations.citation_as_written: North Carolina Rule of Civil Procedure 4(j)(6)(a)
citations.cited_for: Service on a domestic or foreign corporation by delivering a copy of the summons and complaint to a registered agent
citations.context: Service was made in accordance with North Carolina Rule of Civil Procedure 4(j)(6)(a), by delivering a copy of the summons and complaint to a registered agent of a domestic or foreign corporation.

first_check.explanation: N.C. R. Civ. P. 4(j)(6)(a) covers service on a corporation by delivery to an officer, director, or managing agent, or by leaving copies in that person's office. Delivery to an agent authorized by appointment or by law, such as a registered agent, falls under sub-subdivision (b). The rule is real, but the cited sub-subdivision does not describe the method of service the affidavit relies on. This is arguably only a wrong-subsection defect, but in an affidavit of service the subsection identifies the method used, so it matters.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: a. By delivering a copy of the summons and of the complaint to an officer, director, or managing agent of the corporation ... b. By delivering a copy of the summons and of the complaint to an agent authorized by appointment or by law to be served or to accept service of process

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. I read the official N.C.G.S. § 1A-1, Rule 4 text on ncleg.gov. Rule 4(j)(6)a covers "delivering a copy of the summons and of the complaint to an officer, director, or managing agent of the corporation or by leaving copies thereof in the office of such officer..." Delivery to a registered agent is in sub-subdivision b: "delivering a copy ... to an agent authorized by appointment or by law to be served or to accept service of process." The affidavit ties 4(j)(6)(a) to "delivering a copy ... to a registered agent," a method that subdivision does not contain. One point softens the defect. The affidavit says Ms. Whitfield is also the "Corporate Secretary," an officer, so service on her could probably be sustained under (a) on a different theory than the one the affidavit states. Even so, the citation is attached to a method it does not describe, so it is mischaracterized. It is essentially a wrong-sub-subdivision error, and the correct cite for the stated method is Rule 4(j)(6)b.

citations.cited_for: Rubric says it caps exemplary damages at the amount of actual damages, not a 'double damages' multiplier
citations.context: flags that this is an imprecise or misleading characterization of O.C.G.A. § 10-1-763, which caps exemplary damages at the amount of actual damages (not a 'double damages' multiplier)

first_check.quote_check: "double damages" and "double the actual damages" are not in the statute, which uses "twice any award made under subsection (a)". "double the actual damages" is found verbatim in complaint ¶107. "double damages" does not appear verbatim in the complaint.
first_check.explanation: The rubric says § 10-1-763 caps exemplary damages at the amount of actual damages, not a double multiplier. The statute says the opposite: under § 10-1-763(b), exemplary damages may not exceed twice the compensatory award under subsection (a). The rubric therefore misstates the cap. The complaint's 'double' wording is substantively right, and its $3.4M exemplary claim is within the statutory limit.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: (b) If willful and malicious misappropriation exists, the court may award exemplary damages in an amount not exceeding twice any award made under subsection (a) of this Code section.

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. The citing source is the task rubric (task.json ISSUE_004). It says O.C.G.A. § 10-1-763 "caps exemplary damages at the amount of actual damages (not a 'double damages' multiplier)." The statute says the opposite. § 10-1-763(b) reads: "If willful and malicious misappropriation exists, the court may award exemplary damages in an amount not exceeding twice any award made under subsection (a) of this Code section." The cap is twice the compensatory award, not equal to it. The complaint's paragraph 107 says "not exceeding double the actual damages," which is substantively right, apart from cross-referencing § 10-1-762 (injunctive relief) where it should reference § 10-1-763(a). The $3.4M exemplary claim is within the cap. The rubric's 'double damages' quotes do appear in the complaint, but the rubric's statement of the statute's rule is wrong.
